sections.heading: Venerable Martyr Dometios the Persian, and his two disciples

pairs.en: On the same day, the seventh of the month, we remember the holy venerable martyr DOMETIOS the Persian, and his two disciples.
*Beyond all else, Father, it seems you trained your initiates* *to contend at your side by stones.* *With two of his initiates, on the seventh Dometios was set free.*

This saint lived in the reign of the emperor Constantine the Great, in the year 318, and he came from Persia. He was catechised by a Christian named Abaros, and once he had been taught the faith of Christ, he renounced at once his father's ungodliness, and every other pull of his kinsfolk, and so he went to the city called Nisibis, which lies on the frontier between the lands of the Romans and the lands of the Persians.

There the saint entered a monastery, and once he was baptised, put on the habit of the monks, and took up every kind of struggle and asceticism. But because, through the working of the evil demon, the monks there grew envious of him, he left and went to the monastery of the holy martyrs Sergios and Bakchos, in the city called after Theodosios, and there he followed the virtuous way of life of the abbot and archimandrite Ourbil, who is said never, in sixty years, to have eaten cooked food, nor lain down on a bed, nor sat.

For this he was chosen by him and ordained deacon; and when the abbot was about to advance him further, to the rank of priest, Saint Dometios found this out and went away, and climbed up onto a mountain, where the man of blessed memory endured the heat of summer and the cold of winter, and all the other hardships that changes of season bring.

After that he went into a cave made by human hands, and stayed there a good while; and to those who came to him he did good with miracles and cures, which he worked in the name of the Lord, while the unbelievers and pagans he turned from the error of idols to the faith of Christ.

When the apostate emperor Julian learned of this, on his way to make war on Persia, he ordered the saint to be stoned. But when the men sent to stone him arrived, they found him singing the Third Hour together with his two disciples. So with a hail of stones the wretched men buried the athlete of Christ, together with his two disciples, and all three won the crowns of their contest. Their gathering and feast is kept at their own church, which lies across the water at Ioustinianai. (Note that the Greek account of this venerable martyr's contest survives in the Great Lavra; it begins: “The land of Persia bore this good thing too.”)
The venerable OR died in peace.
*Or has left the earth — his grace, he tells us,* *has outgrown your own hour now, O Time.*

sections.heading: The Ten Thousand Ascetics of the Thebaid

pairs.en: The venerable TEN THOUSAND ascetics of the Thebaid died in peace.
*You lead forth from the earth — if David's word may be used —* *your chariot ten-thousand strong, O Word.*
The venerable POTAMIA the wonderworker died by the sword.
*Wonderfully slain by the sword for God's sake,* *Potamia pours out rivers of wonders.*
The holy hieromartyr NARCISSUS, Patriarch of Jerusalem, died by the sword.
*Breathing sweetly, Narcissus, sweeter than the narcissus flower,* *you scent the very garden of Eden.*

In the Dodekabiblos of Dositheos, page 26, this is written about this Narcissus: that once, when the lamp-oil ran out, he found and brought water for the lamps instead, and having prayed and blessed the water, he changed it into oil. He was then falsely accused by three lying denouncers, who could not bear his rebukes and warnings. The first swore a false oath that if he were not telling the truth, he should be burned by fire; the second, that if he were lying, his whole body should be eaten by worms; the third, that if what he said were not true, he should go blind. By these men, I say, the saint was slandered, and he withdrew to a place of stillness, and stayed there many years. But God gave the accusers their just deserts. The first he burned to death, house and family together, exactly as the man had asked for himself; the second he made rot with worms all over, until he was eaten alive by them; and the third, seeing God's vengeance, openly confessed his sin and the false charge that he and his two companions had brought against the most holy Narcissus — and from the many tears he shed, weeping for his sin, his sight failed and he went blind, exactly as he had asked.

This saint lived beyond a hundred and sixteen years, and was patriarch for twenty of them. He held the see of Jerusalem, after James the Brother of God, as its thirtieth bishop — or, by another count, its thirty-first. He was patriarch a second time as well, with Alexander of Jerusalem as his helper — the same Alexander who is kept on the twelfth of December. A little later the godly Narcissus met a martyr's end, and Alexander alone remained.
The holy martyr ASTERIOS the wonderworker died by the sword.
*His neck cut through by the sword, Asterios* *shines among the choirs of martyrs like a star.*
Our venerable father HYPERECHIOS died in peace.
*Hyperechios, though hidden in the tomb,* *has become equal to the choirs of Angels.*

This venerable Hyperechios left us this saying worth remembering: “He who does not govern his tongue in a time of anger will not govern his passions either.” And again he said: “Fasting is a bridle for the monk against sin; whoever throws it off will find himself a lust-mad horse.” The same Hyperechios, in the Paradise of the Fathers, also said this: “A wakeful monk turns night into day, sitting at his prayer; and pricking his own heart, he pours out tears, and calls down mercy from heaven.” He said again: “Just as the lion is fearsome to wild asses, so is the tested monk to sinful thoughts.”
Saint SOZON of Nicomedia, who was thrown into the fire and came out unharmed, died in peace.
*The martyr Sozon proved a second salamander against the flame —* *his end came, but not by fire.*
The venerable and wonder-working THEODOSIOS the New, who lived in the year 862, died in peace.
*New only in his time, this Theodosios* *was, in everything else, the equal of the old.*

sections.heading: Venerable Dometios the Wonder-bearer, of Philotheou

pairs.en: The venerable DOMETIOS the Wonder-bearer, who lived the ascetic life within the bounds of Philotheou monastery, died in peace.
*You were counted worthy to work signs, all-blessed* *Dometios, a very hearth of grace.*
We remember our venerable and God-bearing father NIKANOR the wonderworker, who shone out on Mount Kallistratos.
*Having conquered the world, and all its sweetness,* *you truly carried off the finest victory, Nikanor.*
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
